messages.subject: spatial model with survey weight
parts:
Hello,

I want to fit a spatial model based on individual survey data and consider the survey weights for each individual in the model to achieve more accurate estimates of regional-level values.

y_ij  ~ a_i + b_i * X1_ij + c_i * X2_ij

where y_ij is the response variable for the individual j in the area i. As my current understanding, I can set the weights using the `weights` argument in the `inla` function. However, I have two questions that I am confused about: Does the `weights` argument in the `inla` function only adjust the model's beta coefficients? And regarding the `summary.fitted.values` obtained after fitting the model, are the individual fitted values adjusted based on the survey weights? Is it more accurate to obtain regional estimates by summing and averaging the individual i fitted values obtained after fitting the model that considers survey weights compared to the model that does not consider survey weights?

Can you please help clarify?

inla.setOption("enable.inla.argument.weights", TRUE)

formula<-Yij~ 1 + X1_ij + X2_ij +

  f(area,

    model = "iid",

    hyper=list(theta=list(prior="loggamma",param=c(1,0.05))))

result <-

  inla(formula,family="gaussian",data=final,verbose = F, weights =data$weight

       control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,waic=T,cpo=TRUE,config=TRUE),

       control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),

       control.inla=list(strategy='auto', int.strategy='eb'))

fit_yij <-result $summary.fitted.values[1]

messages.author: d560d9e01924933c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial model with survey weight
parts:
Hi Claire,

Unfortunately you cannot use the sampling weights in the weights argument in INLA (or any other software/method).

One fast and simple alternative is the use of pseudo posterior, where the sum of weights should be equal the sample size.  So in your code you should redefine the weights as

# assuming length(data$weights) is the sample size

# backup of original sampling weights
data$weights2 = data$weights
# recalculating the weights
data$weights = data$weights2 / sum(data$weights2) * length (data$weights2 )

# then, you can use your code using the new weights in the weights argument.

messages.author: d560d9e01924933c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial model with survey weight
parts:
Hi Claire,

It os not only for the beta coefficients but for all parameters because the weights are going to be applied directly into the likelihood function.

The weights argument in INLA is the usual weights argument in several functions and packages. It is used when you have aggregated data, each line on your dataset is not an individual but several of them (the number is given by the weights). So if you use the sampling weights on the weights argument in the software would understand that each observation occurs a quite large number of times and your actual sample size would be the population size (given by the sum of sampling weights).

You could have a look at any survey book, I like the one from Prof Thomas Lumley based on the survey R package.
https://r-survey.r-forge.r-project.org/svybook/

The use of survey weights in Bayesian statistics is complicated. There are some approaches but they all seem to be messy. The simplest one in my humble opinion is this Pseudo Bayesian approach proposed by Savitsky and others. So from his paper I figured that to use shaming weights in Inla you should just do this trick with the sampling weights.

Here it is the Savitsky and Toth (2016) https://projecteuclid.org/journals/electronic-journal-of-statistics/volume-10/issue-1/Bayesian-estimation-under-informative-sampling/10.1214/16-EJS1153.full

As I said this approach works, but you may get in trouble with "very religious" people from both groups Bayesians and Survey statisticians. :-)

I hope that helps.

Cheers,
Leo
